Abstract The forecasting and early warning of flash floods in mountainous areas are extremely
challenging. Here, we establish an integrated model of Baseflow‐Rainfall‐Interception‐Flood (BRIF) to support
efficient numerical modeling and potential forecasting of flash flood in future. The local inertia approximation
equations and the heterogeneous parallel computing scheme of CPU + GPU adopted in the BRIF model have
realized a high performance and robustness solver, and the generability across frameworks has been completed
with low cost and high efficiency. The findings suggest that the local inertia approximation equations remain a
viable solution for simulating flash floods using heterogeneous parallel computing methods. For purpose of
potential application in forecast and early warning, we develop a model that utilizes land‐use types to determine
the underlying surface parameters. The possibility risk of flash flood is proposed to be evaluated by comparing
predicted discharge with the peak flow during the return period discharge curve. The efficiency of the BRIF
model has been verified by comparing with the analytical solution and multiple real flash flood events. It is
shown the speedup (the computational time verse the rainfall procedure) is several to tens of times in a high‐
resolution grid. Thus, the current BRIF model proposed has great potential for flash flood forecasting in future.
1. Introduction
Flooding in mountainous areas is usually serious natural disasters caused by extreme rainfall events. With global
climate change and the increasing frequency of extreme rainfall events (IPCG, 2018; Kirchmeier‐Young
et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2020), flood induced disasters have become an issue of global
concern (Diakakis et al., 2020; Fekete & Sandholz, 2021; Yang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2024). Furthermore,
flooding is more unpredictable in mountainous areas than in urban areas and large rivers due to its rapid evolution
and insufficient data (Lin et al., 2021; Montesarchio et al., 2011). Thus, the monitoring and prediction of flood
evolution at the catchment scale are essential for developing flood risk reduction measures. The most reliable
approach toward flood disaster prevention is to install various instruments and equipment in catchments.
However, owing to investment and maintenance issues, monitoring devices are lacking in the overwhelming
majority of catchments in mountainous areas.
The advancements in numerical weather prediction (NWP) in recent years have been remarkable, enabling the
provision of products with a resolution as fine as hourly and at the kilometer level (Bauer et al., 2015; Bisht
et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2022). Currently, the early‐warning and prediction of floods in mountainous area are
mainly based on the rainfall threshold from rain gauge networks or weather forecast systems (Borga et al., 2014;
Kauffeldt et al., 2016; Montesarchio et al., 2011). However, the key barrier preventing its efficient applicability is
that the rainfall threshold value may widely vary in different catchments. The discharge and water depth can
reflect the geographical characteristics of each small‐ungauged catchment with narrow channels. Thus the
discharge ratio and water depth threshold derived from numerical prediction of the entire physical process of
rainfall to flood is an important addition and a potential game‐changer in the future as the versatility of its physical
mechanism (Bout & Jetten, 2017; Shen et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2024).
To better simulate flood routing processes, two‐dimensional shallow water equations (SWEs) have been
extensively developed in flood simulation (Audusse et al., 2004; Costabile et al., 2009; Liang et al., 2016; Xia &
Liang, 2018). However, some problems of computational efficiency remain in solving flash flood forecasting. To

In this regard, some simplified forms of SWEs with a simpler flux calculation method have also been developed,
such as the kinematic wave model (Park et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2017) and diffusive wave model (Kazezyılmaz‐
Alhan, 2012; Savant et al., 2019; Su et al., 2017). Bates et al. (2010) proposed the local inertial approximation
form model (LIM, i.e. LISFLOOD‐ACC, Neal et al., 2012, 2018), which retains the local inertial term of SWEs
and improves the stability (Cea & Blade, 2015; Wang, Jiang, et al., 2021), and can produce results comparable to
SWEs with lower computational cost (Martins et al., 2017). The application of the local inertial approximation
form model focuses on the simulation of urban floods with relatively gentle terrain conditions (Wang, Chen, &
Huang, 2021), and its applicability in steep, small mountainous catchment is close to surpass the limit of neglected
advection term.
In recent years, the application of GPUs to accelerate computation has become increasingly more popular (Dazzi
et al., 2020; Morales‐Hernández et al., 2021; Xing et al., 2019). The common CPU + GPU hardware structure is
shown in Figure 1. Parallel processing based on GPUs (Graphics Processing Units) is widely being adopted to
improve computational efficiency. Sætra and Brodtkorb (2012) explores the benefits of domain decomposition in
utilization which provide a reference for applying calculations to multi‐GPU. Liang's team realized real‐time
simulation of urban/flash flood events based on SWEs using in‐house multi‐GPU computers (Liang
et al., 2016; Ming et al., 2020; Xia et al., 2019). Kalyanapu realized 15 times the simulation speed of real events
based on GPU improvements (Kalyanapu et al., 2011). Dullo et al. (2021) adopted a first‐order upwind scheme to
solve the two‐dimensional SWEs with source term and realized high performance of the program. Lacasta
et al. (2015) realized the solution of the SWEs of an unstructured grid based on GPU. With the iterative update of
computer hardware, especially the development of supercomputing, the boost from hardware improvements is
enormous (Caviedes‐Voullième et al., 2023; Wang, Jiang, et al., 2021).
In this paper, our team is developing a handy flash flood simulation tool for mountainous small catchments based
on a 2‐D hydrodynamic model. We aim to create a high‐performance and performance‐portable model that can be
applied to real flood warning and forecast operations. For this purpose, the local inertial approximation form
model was taken to simulate the dynamic process of flash floods at the catchment scale. Further, CPU + GPU
heterogeneous parallel technology is introduced to improve the computational efficiency. The high robustness
and performance of the model was verified through two model tests and application in two real mountainous small
catchments.

2. Model Framework
Figure 2 shows the BRIF model framework, which mainly includes three modules: data module, dynamic
simulation module, and analytical result module. First, the data module includes the basic inputs required to drive
the physical model, such as terrain and rainfall, land‐use types, and soil depth. The dynamic simulation module is
based on local inertia approximation equations to simulate the BRIF process of flash floods. Finally, the model
generates the maximum water depth and velocity, which is further create a flood inundation map to evaluate the
danger of the watershed space during this rainfall‐flood process. The predicted discharge will be compared with
the peak flow which is calculated during the return period to obtain the peak flow ratio. Furthermore, the
dangerous risk of the entire rainfall event is evaluated based on this ratio.

Second, for hundreds of catchments in a large region, it is necessary to complete the simulation in a short time.
Meanwhile, the tool may run on devices of different platforms, which requires the tool to have high performance
and portability. In other words, faster computation times allow earlier release of warning signals, and performance‐
portable gives the tool stronger vitality. On the one hand, we all know that the local inertia approximation equation
has advantages over SWEs in terms of convenience on explicit solutions, and its applicability to flash flood is
verified by subsequent model experiments. On the other hand, the advantages of both CPUs and GPUs can be
harnessed by developing heterogeneous designs based on their combination. Efficient computation is essential for
early warning and high‐quality dynamic simulation data for artificial intelligence (An et al., 2025; Najafi
et al., 2024).
Regarding performance portability, there are currently two main strategies for addressing performance portability
issues: one is to build an intermediate layer that provides a unified programming interface such as Raja (https://
github.com/LLNL/RAJA) and Kokkos (https://github.com/kokkos/kokkos); another approach is to delegate the
task to the compiler HIPIFY (https://github.com/ROCm/HIPIFY). HIP (Heterogeneous‐Compute Interface for

matically convert source from CUDA (Compute Unified Device Architecture, a general‐purpose parallel
computing platform. https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda‐toolkit) to ROCm (Radeon Open Compute Platform, an
open source heterogeneous computing platform. https://www.amd.com/rocm). For exploration, as shown in

5. Conclusions and Outlook
The early warning and prediction of flash floods based on numerical modeling of the entire physical process is of
high significance for risk management. This article establishes a BRIF model with high performance and
transferability that can be used for flash flood forecasting in mountainous small catchment. The simplified model
of SWEs and the heterogeneous parallel computing scheme of CPU + GPU adopted by BRIF model have realized
a high‐performance and highly robust solver for the two‐dimensional local inertial approximation equation, and
the generability across frameworks has been completed with very low cost and efficiency by using the HIPIFY
tool. The results indicate that even for the performance of current advanced computer hardware devices, the local
inertia approximation equation based on heterogeneous parallel computing methods is still an effective solution
for predicting flash flood in mountainous small catchment.
For physical models, this article introduces vegetation interception and channel base flow bottom on the tradi-
tional rainfall infiltration runoff process to improve the response speed and accuracy of the model to the rainfall‐
runoff process. Numerical experiments have shown that the impact of base flow on runoff cannot be ignored when
rainfall is concentrated in the forward pattern. On the other hand, in the actual operation process of the BRIF
model, when facing a large number of small watersheds without underlying surface data, it is required that the
prediction model maintain good transferability. In terms of model application, we have established a model for
determining the underlying surface parameters based on land‐use types, and evaluated the flash flood risk of the
watershed by the peak flow ratio. The inversion results of the BRIF model on the actual flash flood events in the
Heishuigou area show that the model can accurately determine the risk of flash floods. This also reflects that the
model has the potential to predict flash flood risk.
When proposing this high‐performance flash flood prediction model, the author still has some deeper thinking, so
here are some prospects based on flash flood prediction research. For model parameters, authentic data is critical
to simulation, but it is often challenging to get complete data in forecasting. The current underlying surface
parameter adopted in the paper is only a relatively rough and convenient solution. In the later stage, with the
upgrading of investigation methods and the enrichment of experimental data, parameters can be further modified
for different research areas. The quality of forecast rainfall data largely determines the accuracy of flash flood risk

Abstract: The forecasting and early warning of flash floods in mountainous areas are extremely challenging. Here, we establish an integrated model of Baseflow‐Rainfall‐Interception‐Flood (BRIF) to support efficient numerical modeling and potential forecasting of flash flood in future. The local inertia approximation equations and the heterogeneous parallel computing scheme of CPU + GPU adopted in the BRIF model have realized a high performance and robustness solver, and the generability across frameworks has been completed with low cost and high efficiency. The findings suggest that the local inertia approximation equations remain a viable solution for simulating flash floods using heterogeneous parallel computing methods. For purpose of potential application in forecast and early warning, we develop a model that utilizes land‐use types to determine the underlying surface parameters. The possibility risk of flash flood is proposed to be evaluated by comparing predicted discharge with the peak flow during the return period discharge curve. The efficiency of the BRIF model has been verified by comparing with the analytical solution and multiple real flash flood events. It is shown the speedup (the computational time verse the rainfall procedure) is several to tens of times in a high‐ resolution grid. Thus, the current BRIF model proposed has great potential for flash flood forecasting in future.
